title: Houthis claim missile strikes on Riyadh as fuel depot burns at airport
excerpt: Yemen's Iran-backed rebels say they fired ballistic and cruise missiles and drones at "sensitive sites" in the Saudi capital and Aramco facilities in Yanbu; Riyadh says its air defenses intercepted the attacks, but a burning fuel tank at King Khalid airport tells its own story.
body:
• Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed on Saturday, September 19, that they carried out two military operations against "sensitive sites" in Riyadh and Aramco facilities in the Red Sea port of Yanbu, using what they called a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones.
  • Saudi authorities issued overnight warnings of a "hostile aerial threat" over Riyadh and nearby Al-Kharj; a fuel depot near King Khalid International Airport caught fire, sending black smoke over the capital, while flight operations were temporarily disrupted.
  • The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile headed for Riyadh early Saturday and thwarted additional attempts against civilians and infrastructure in Bisha, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu.
  • The Houthis said the strikes retaliated for Saudi attacks on Yemen's capital Sanaa — the first direct assault on Riyadh in months and a sharp escalation in the region's widening confrontation.

Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed Saturday that they had launched missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia's capital, hours after flames and a towering plume of black smoke rose from a fuel depot near Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement on Telegram that the group executed two operations — one targeting what he called "sensitive" locations in Riyadh, the other aimed at facilities belonging to oil giant Aramco in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.

Saudi officials did not confirm the Houthi claims when the reports were published. But three officials with knowledge of the incident told the Wall Street Journal that the strike hit jet-fuel facilities at the airfield, and an AFP journalist watched firefighters extinguish a burning fuel tank bearing the Aramco logo at a depot near the airport. Reuters footage showed thick smoke rising near the airport with flames visible behind what appeared to be fuel storage tanks. Flight-tracking service FlightRadar24 temporarily reported major disruption at Riyadh airport before traffic began returning to normal.

"The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu."

— Yahya Saree, Houthi military spokesperson, in a Telegram statement

The Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson, Col. Turki al-Malki, said the kingdom's air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh in the early hours of Saturday. He said additional Houthi attempts against civilians and infrastructure in Bisha, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu were also thwarted. In a statement on X, the coalition described the attacks as "terrorist and aggressive behavior," accusing the rebels of trying to target civilians. No casualties were immediately reported.

Context & Background

The assault marks the first direct strike on Riyadh in months and a dangerous turn in a conflict that has been steadily widening. The Houthis have spent recent weeks squeezing Saudi Arabia's Red Sea export routes, and the kingdom has been targeted in attacks launched from both Yemen and Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate. The rebels accused Saudi Arabia of earlier strikes on Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, that they said provoked Saturday's assault.

Tensions have been compounding for weeks. Days earlier, Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting the holy city of Mecca — a claim the rebels dismissed as a "worn-out lie." Earlier this month, the UN Security Council convened after an earlier round of strikes wounded 73 people in southern Saudi Arabia, with UN envoy Hans Grundberg warning that Yemen risked falling back into full-scale war for the first time since the 2022 truce.

Impact & Analysis

Striking at Riyadh's airport and Yanbu — a port city housing a refinery and an oil export terminal linked to the kingdom's East-West pipeline — the Houthis are pressing on Saudi Arabia's economic pressure points. Yanbu's role in bypassing the Strait of Hormuz makes it a particularly sensitive target, and any sustained threat to Saudi export infrastructure reverberates through global oil markets.

The episode also exposes the fog that now surrounds each exchange. Riyadh's account emphasizes interceptions and thwarted attempts; the Houthis claim "successful" strikes with massive fires. The burning fuel depot at the airport gives the rebels' version visible weight, even as Saudi authorities have not publicly confirmed that the fire resulted directly from a missile or drone impact.

"Terrorist and aggressive behavior."

— Saudi-led coalition statement, on the Houthi attacks

Diaspora Angle

Saudi Arabia hosts millions of Indian workers, and any escalation that reaches the capital raises direct safety concerns for the diaspora — Indian missions in the kingdom have issued advisories during past flare-ups, and families back home will be watching Riyadh's skies closely.

What's Next

The critical question is whether Saturday was a one-off retaliation or the start of a sustained campaign against the Saudi heartland. A return to regular strikes on Riyadh would mark the collapse of the fragile calm that held since the 2022 truce and could draw sharper American involvement in a conflict Washington has tried to keep at arm's length. For now, both sides are claiming the upper hand — and the burned fuel tank at King Khalid airport is the one fact nobody disputes.
